summary: Specifies a minimum set of requirements for Uniform Resource Names (URNs), a kind of resource identifier that stays the same even when the resource moves. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1737 lists requirements for Uniform Resource Names, which identify resources without naming their current location. A URN should remain unique and persistent, while a separate mechanism can help find a location where the resource is available.

questions: what are the requirements for a urn
subtitle: The functional and encoding requirements for permanent, location-independent resource names.

tldr.problem: A location can change or disappear even when a resource remains identifiable, so a lasting identifier must not be tied to one location.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists functional and encoding requirements for Uniform Resource Names, including uniqueness, persistence, simple comparison, transport, and resolution to a URL.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1737 is an Informational basis for evaluating URN specifications. It leaves resource equality, visible name meaning, and the details of resolution to other services or authorities.

today: RFC 1737 is an Informational memo published in December 1994. It provides requirements for evaluating URN specifications and does not itself specify an Internet standard.

sections.title: Names, Characteristics and Locations
sections.content:
The memo places Uniform Resource Names (URNs), Uniform Resource Characteristics (URCs), and Uniform Resource Locators (URLs) in one information architecture. A URN identifies a resource, a URC carries information about it, and a URL identifies a location or container where an instance may be found.

A resource may have several locations, move, or be unavailable. RFC 1737 therefore describes a URN as a globally unique, persistent identifier for recognition or access to information about a resource or to the resource itself. These requirements form a basis for evaluating URN specifications; the memo says they are not exhaustive.
sections.plainLanguage: A URN identifies a resource, while a URL identifies a place where a copy may be found. The resource can move or be unavailable without changing what the URN identifies.

sections.title: Requirements for What a URN Can Do
sections.content:
The memo lists eight functional requirements. A URN must have global scope and uniqueness, and its lifetime is intended to be permanent. The scheme should scale to resources that may be available on a network for hundreds of years, allow legacy naming systems and future extensions, and leave name-issuing conditions to the issuing authority.

A URN must also not impede resolution to a URL. If a corresponding URL exists, there must be a feasible way to translate the URN into that URL. The memo encourages naming authorities to arrange such mappings but does not require the authority itself to operate them.
sections.plainLanguage: A URN should mean the same thing everywhere and never identify two different resources. It should also be possible to translate it into a URL when a location for the resource is available.

sections.title: Requirements for Writing and Comparing URNs
sections.content:
The encoding for people to read and transmit must be the same. Comparison must use a simple, local, deterministic algorithm that needs no external server. The name should be short, use few special characters, and be case-insensitive enough to support accurate human transcription.

A URN must pass unmodified through common Internet protocols and be printable on paper. It must be machine-parseable, and its format should make it easy to recognize and parse in free text. The memo does not require people to generate or interpret the meaning of a URN.
sections.plainLanguage: A URN should be easy to copy, send, and compare. Computers must be able to parse it, and its form should make it recognizable inside ordinary text.

sections.title: How Naming Authorities Support Uniqueness
sections.content:
The memo concludes that naming authorities can help meet uniqueness and scale requirements. An authority can assign names itself or delegate part of its naming space to sub-authorities. Each authority is responsible for keeping its assigned names unique, while top-level authorities are centrally registered.

The memo says authorities should limit the character set so names can be transcribed and sent by mail, although it notes that there was no consensus on the exact limit. It also recommends a mapping from names to URLs, which may return zero or more locations at a given time.
sections.plainLanguage: Naming authorities divide responsibility for assigning names and keeping them unique. A URN may map to no location or to several locations at a given time.

sections.title: Questions the Memo Leaves Open
sections.content:
RFC 1737 does not decide how to determine whether two resources are equal. Different naming authorities may choose different comparison rules for the resources they name. It also does not require that a URN's visible characters reveal information about the resource, though it discourages relying on such meaning because it may change.

The memo does not specify how name resolution works. It recommends a translation mechanism for each authority and encourages third-party or distributed resolver services. Authentication information about a name or resource should generally travel separately from the URN.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo leaves each naming authority to decide which resources count as the same. It also leaves resolver design open and recommends carrying authentication information separately from the name.

viz.caption: THE EIGHT FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS IN RFC 1737

items.title: Global scope
items.text: The name has the same meaning everywhere and implies no location.

items.title: Global uniqueness
items.text: The same URN is not assigned to two different resources.

items.title: Persistence
items.text: The name is intended to remain permanent.

items.title: Scalability
items.text: The scheme can name resources over hundreds of years.

items.title: Legacy support
items.text: Existing naming systems can be embedded when they meet the requirements.

items.title: Independence
items.text: The issuing authority sets its own conditions for issuing names.

items.title: Resolution
items.text: A URN does not impede translation to a URL.
